contradictions.question: When was heaven created?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:1 places the creation of heaven at the very beginning, before anything else, while Genesis 1:6-8 has God making a firmament on the second day and naming it Heaven. Matthew 25:34 and John 14:2 push the timing elsewhere entirely, implying heaven was prepared from the foundation of the world or is still being prepared by Jesus after his ascension.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction hits the text on two levels. First, Genesis itself can't agree with Genesis. The Priestly author in Genesis 1:1 uses shamayim to cover the entire created cosmos 'in the beginning,' then five verses later has that same Heaven appearing on day two as a solid dome separating the upper and lower waters. That's not one smooth narrative, it's two different cosmological ideas stacked on top of each other. Second, the New Testament layers a distinctly different Heaven on top of that, one that functions as a prepared dwelling for the righteous rather than a physical sky. Apologists typically resolve this by distinguishing between 'heaven' as the atmospheric sky (day two), 'heaven' as outer space (also day two, or day four), and 'heaven' as God's throne room (uncreated, or pre-existent). Gleason Archer takes exactly this path in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. The problem is that this three-heavens framework is a post-hoc rationalization read back into Genesis. The Priestly author had one cosmology: a flat earth under a solid raqia. The later apocalyptic and Pauline three-heavens scheme (2 Cor 12:2) is a Second Temple development, not a Genesis concept. That is a subjective call on the evidence, but the evidence leans hard toward the authors simply not agreeing.
contradictions.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Priestly Vision of Genesis 1 (Fortress, 2010), pp. 71-79, on the raqia and Priestly cosmology. John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (IVP Academic, 2009), pp. 55-71, on ancient cosmic geography. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 59-60, for the harmonizing 'three heavens' response. Jon D. Levenson, Creation and the Persistence of Evil (Princeton, 1994), pp. 3-13, on the Priestly cosmogony. Raymond E. Brown, The Gospel According to John (AB 29A; Doubleday, 1966), pp. 620-621, on the eschatological 'mansions' of John 14:2.

contradictions.question: Who created heaven and earth?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:1 and Isaiah 44:24 state that God the Father created everything alone, explicitly stretching out the heavens 'by myself.' John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 instead attribute creation to Jesus, through whom 'all things were created.' 1 Corinthians 8:6 tries to split the job, assigning creation 'from' the Father and 'through' the Son.
contradictions.commentary: This one exposes a fault line running through New Testament Christology. The Hebrew Bible is emphatic that YHWH acts alone. Isaiah 44:24 isn't subtle. The Hebrew lebaddi means 'by myself, alone,' and mei'itti means 'from myself,' with nobody else involved. Deutero-Isaiah is polemically monotheistic, and the whole point of that passage is that there was no co-creator. Then you get to John's prologue and Colossians, and suddenly the Logos/Christ is the agent through whom everything is made. Apologists like Craig Blomberg and Wayne Grudem harmonize this through Trinitarian theology: the Father creates through the Son by the Spirit, so all three are involved in one creative act. The problem is that Trinitarian theology is a fourth-century development, not a first-century one, and it doesn't actually match what Isaiah 44:24 is claiming. Isaiah is denying that any second party was involved, not distinguishing roles within a single divine being. Larry Hurtado and Bart Ehrman have both traced how high Christology developed by attributing OT divine prerogatives to Jesus, which is exactly what Colossians 1:16 does. That is of course a subjective call, but the evidence points to theological evolution, not a unified doctrine present from the beginning.
contradictions.scholarship: Larry W. Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ: Devotion to Jesus in Earliest Christianity (Eerdmans, 2003), pp. 27-78, on early exaltation Christology. Bart D. Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (HarperOne, 2014), pp. 251-282. James D. G. Dunn, Christology in the Making (Eerdmans, 1996), pp. 187-196, on Colossians and Wisdom Christology. Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the God of Israel (Eerdmans, 2008), pp. 18-31, for the Trinitarian harmonization via divine identity. John J. Collins, Introduction to the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2018), pp. 388-393, on Deutero-Isaiah's monotheism.

contradictions.question: When were the stars made?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:16-19 has God making the stars on the fourth day of creation, after the earth already existed. Job 38:4-7 pictures the 'morning stars' already singing together when God laid the earth's foundations, placing the stars before the earth.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction plays out between genre registers, but it still sits awkwardly. Genesis 1 is a structured Priestly cosmogony with a clear sequence: earth on day three, luminaries including stars on day four. Job 38 is poetic speech, but the cosmological picture it paints has the stars (or angelic 'sons of God' associated with stars) already present and celebrating when the earth gets founded. Apologists commonly argue Job 38 is poetry and shouldn't be pressed for chronology, or that 'morning stars' there refers to angels rather than literal stars, pointing to the parallelism with 'sons of God' (bene elohim). That's not a bad move, and it's the line Gleason Archer and John Walton take. But the poetic/literal split doesn't eliminate the problem, because even if 'morning stars' means angels, the passage still presents stars as part of the cosmological furniture before the earth is founded. And the Genesis 1 sequence itself is a known ancient Near Eastern oddity. Mark Smith notes that the Priestly author is adapting a schema where the luminaries are deliberately demoted from their usual divine status, so they get delayed to day four as functional objects rather than beings. That is a subjective read, but the tension is real either way.
contradictions.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Priestly Vision of Genesis 1 (Fortress, 2010), pp. 83-85, on the demotion of luminaries. Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis (JPS Torah Commentary, 1989), pp. 8-9. Pope, Job (AB 15; Doubleday, 1965), pp. 293-294, on 'morning stars' in Job 38:7.

contradictions.question: When did God divide light from darkness?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:4-5 says God divided light from darkness on the first day of creation, before any celestial bodies existed. Genesis 1:16-19 then has God creating the sun, moon, and stars on the fourth day and using them to divide light from darkness.
contradictions.commentary: This one is almost self-refuting because both verses are inside the same chapter and use essentially the same Hebrew phrase: lehavdil bein ha-or u'vein ha-choshek, 'to divide between the light and the darkness.' Day one does the dividing. Day four does the dividing again, this time with the luminaries as the mechanism. Apologists like Archer usually argue that day one refers to primordial light (maybe God's own glory or some pre-solar cosmic light) and day four is just when God instituted the regular rhythm through the sun and moon. That's a workable reading if you assume Genesis 1 was composed as a single tight cosmology, but it isn't. Mark Smith and the mainstream of Pentateuchal scholarship recognize that the Priestly author is building a liturgical-cosmological structure in which days one through three create domains and days four through six fill them. That structural parallelism is why the 'dividing' gets repeated. The text isn't claiming two different acts of dividing in a unified timeline, it's the Priestly author using the same vocabulary to mark the correspondence between the creation of the environment (day 1) and the creation of the inhabitants of that environment (day 4). The problem is that once you read it as straight chronology, the text contradicts itself, and the ancient author almost certainly didn't care because the structure was the point.
contradictions.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Priestly Vision of Genesis 1 (Fortress, 2010), pp. 87-92, on the domain/inhabitants parallel structure. Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15 (WBC 1; Word, 1987), pp. 6-7. Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary (Fortress, 1984), pp. 112-114. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 60-61, for the two-phase harmonization.

contradictions.question: From what were the fowls created?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:20-21 has God commanding the waters to bring forth birds. Genesis 2:19 instead says God formed every fowl of the air 'out of the ground.' The two creation accounts give the birds two different sources.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest illustrations of the Documentary Hypothesis in the Pentateuch. Genesis 1-2:4a is Priestly material with its characteristic structured cosmogony, where birds emerge from the waters alongside aquatic life. Genesis 2:4b onward is the Yahwistic (J) account, which has a completely different creation order and formation method. In J, YHWH forms animals (including birds) from the adamah, the ground, the same material he uses for the man. Apologists including Archer and Kenneth Mathews typically argue that 'out of the ground' in 2:19 is a general phrase meaning terrestrial origin, or they appeal to the NIV's translational move rendering it as pluperfect ('had formed') to push the event back into chapter one. The pluperfect move is grammatically strained. Hebrew waw-consecutive imperfect doesn't naturally carry pluperfect force here, and the context is clearly sequential: God decides Adam needs a helper, so he then forms the animals to see if any fit. That's not a flashback, it's the next step in the narrative. Kugel, Friedman, and Collins all treat this as a textbook case of two independent creation traditions spliced together. The contradiction is built into the seam.
contradictions.scholarship: Richard Elliott Friedman, The Bible with Sources Revealed (HarperOne, 2003), pp. 33-37, on J vs. P in Genesis 1-2. James L. Kugel, How to Read the Bible (Free Press, 2007), pp. 50-57. John J. Collins, Introduction to the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2018), pp. 73-83. Joel S. Baden, The Composition of the Pentateuch (Yale, 2012), pp. 193-206. Kenneth A. Mathews, Genesis 1-11:26 (NAC 1A; B&H, 1996), pp. 214-216, for the pluperfect harmonization. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 68-69.

contradictions.question: From what were the animals created?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:20 has God commanding the waters to bring forth living creatures. Genesis 2:19 states the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird 'out of the ground.' Two different raw materials for the same animals.
contradictions.commentary: Same fault line as the fowls contradiction, and for the same reason: two independent creation traditions sitting side by side. The Priestly author in Genesis 1 uses a command-fulfillment pattern where God speaks and the elements produce. The Yahwist in Genesis 2 uses a hands-on, artisanal model where YHWH physically molds creatures from dirt. These aren't stylistic variations of one story. They're competing cosmogonies. Harmonizers typically argue that 'ground' is being used loosely, or that the two accounts focus on different aspects (Gen 1 is about origin, Gen 2 is about formation for Adam's sake), so they don't technically contradict. Walton takes this functional-versus-material angle. The problem is that Genesis 2:19 uses the verb yatsar, the same word used for YHWH forming the man from the adamah in 2:7. The author is explicitly paralleling animal formation to human formation. Both come from the ground. That's not a detail about 'focus,' it's a claim about material origin. Friedman, Baden, and the broader source-critical consensus read these as the J and P sources, and the contradiction is exactly the kind of doublet the Documentary Hypothesis predicts.
contradictions.scholarship: Richard Elliott Friedman, The Bible with Sources Revealed (HarperOne, 2003), pp. 33-37. Joel S. Baden, The Composition of the Pentateuch (Yale, 2012), pp. 193-206. John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (IVP Academic, 2009), pp. 85-97, for the functional-ontology harmonization. E. A. Speiser, Genesis (AB 1; Doubleday, 1964), pp. 18-20. Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15 (WBC 1; Word, 1987), pp. 55-56.

contradictions.question: Were humans created before or after the other animals?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:25-27 has God creating the animals first and then creating humans, male and female, on the same day. Genesis 2:18-19 reverses this: the man is formed first, then God forms the animals to see if any of them would be a suitable helper for him.
contradictions.commentary: This is the canonical example of Genesis 1 contradicting Genesis 2, and it's a textbook case for the Documentary Hypothesis. In P (Genesis 1), the sequence is deliberate: plants, sea life and birds, land animals, humans. Humans come last as the climax of creation. In J (Genesis 2), YHWH forms the man first from the dust, plants the garden, then forms the animals after noticing that 'it is not good that the man should be alone' as an attempt to find him a helper. Apologists typically attempt the pluperfect translation move ('had formed,' as in the NIV), arguing that Genesis 2:19 describes animals already created back in Genesis 1. Archer and Mathews both run this play. The grammar doesn't cooperate. The Hebrew wayyitzer is a standard waw-consecutive, which normally expresses narrative sequence, not a flashback. Pushing it to pluperfect is a theologically motivated translation choice, not a linguistically required one. Beyond the grammar, the logic of the J narrative falls apart under the pluperfect reading. If the animals were already made, why would God parade them past Adam to find a helper? The narrative only makes sense if the animals are being freshly formed as candidate companions. James Kugel makes this point bluntly: the two accounts aren't two angles on the same event, they're two traditions that the redactor placed side by side.
contradictions.scholarship: James L. Kugel, How to Read the Bible (Free Press, 2007), pp. 50-57. Richard Elliott Friedman, The Bible with Sources Revealed (HarperOne, 2003), pp. 33-37. Joel S. Baden, The Composition of the Pentateuch (Yale, 2012), pp. 193-206. E. A. Speiser, Genesis (AB 1; Doubleday, 1964), pp. 15-20. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 68-69, for the pluperfect defense. Kenneth A. Mathews, Genesis 1-11:26 (NAC 1A; B&H, 1996), pp. 214-216. Victor P. Hamilton, The Book of Genesis 1-17 (NICOT; Eerdmans, 1990), commentary on Genesis 2:18-20.

contradictions.question: How many gods are there?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and New Testament passages repeatedly assert strict monotheism, with YHWH alone and no other gods beside him. Genesis 1:26, 3:22, and 11:7 have God using first-person plural ('let us make,' 'one of us') and Psalm 82 has God judging in the assembly of gods. The Hebrew Bible carries both currents at once.
contradictions.commentary: The question is slightly coarse as posed, but the contradiction underneath is real and is one of the most important issues in Hebrew Bible scholarship. The later monotheistic texts, especially Deutero-Isaiah (40-55), are polemically insistent that YHWH is the only God. The older material is more complicated. Genesis 1:26's 'let us make man in our image' has been explained as the royal 'we,' as a plural of deliberation, as an address to the angelic court, or as a Trinitarian anticipation. Only two of those are serious. Hebrew has no royal plural of that kind, and Trinitarian readings are a fourth-century retrojection. The strongest reading, carried by Michael Heiser and Mark Smith alike, is that these plurals reflect Israel's older cosmology in which YHWH presides over a divine council of lesser elohim. Psalm 82 makes this explicit: 'God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment.' Apologists including Archer and Daniel Block argue these 'gods' are human judges or angels, never actual deities. The textual data pushes back hard. Deuteronomy 32:8-9, in the Dead Sea Scrolls and LXX reading, has Elyon distributing the nations to the 'sons of God,' with YHWH receiving Israel as his portion. That's a council of gods, not a list of judges. Smith and Collins read the biblical canon as preserving an evolution from polytheism through monolatry to full monotheism, with the seams still visible. That is a subjective call on some passages, but the raw textual evidence for pre-monotheistic Israelite religion is extensive.
contradictions.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (Oxford, 2001), pp. 27-40, 135-148. Mark S. Smith, The Early History of God, 2nd ed. (Eerdmans, 2002), pp. 32-43. contradictions.question: Is childbearing sinful?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:28 and parallel passages command humanity to 'be fruitful and multiply,' framing reproduction as divine mandate. Leviticus 12:6-7 requires a new mother to bring a sin offering to make atonement for herself after childbirth, implying bearing a child renders her ritually impure in a way that needs sacrificial cleansing.
contradictions.commentary: The tension here depends on how you read the term chatat in Leviticus 12. The word is typically translated 'sin offering,' but functionally it serves as a purification offering, cleansing ritual impurity rather than moral guilt. Jacob Milgrom is the scholar who pushed hardest on this distinction, arguing that chatat in the Priestly material addresses pollution of the sanctuary, not personal sin. On that reading, childbirth isn't sinful, it's ritually defiling in the same way corpse contact or menstruation is defiling. Apologists run with this: Archer, Walton, and most evangelical commentators treat the issue as purity-versus-sin, and they have a point. The problem is that even if chatat is 'purification offering,' the text still says the priest 'shall make atonement for her' (kipper), which is the same atonement vocabulary used elsewhere for sin. And the doubled purity period for female children (14 days unclean plus 66 days of purification, versus 7 and 33 for males) isn't easily explained by any pure 'ritual neutrality' reading. James Kugel and Richard Elliott Friedman both note that the Priestly system treats bodily emissions associated with reproduction as intrinsically defiling, which creates an internal tension with the Genesis creation mandate to multiply. That is a subjective call, but the tension between the command to reproduce and the ritual cost of reproduction is real.

contradictions.question: May Adam eat from any tree?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:29 has God giving the humans 'every herb bearing seed' and 'every tree' with seed-bearing fruit for food, without restriction. Genesis 2:17 places one tree explicitly off-limits: the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
contradictions.commentary: This is another P/J seam. Genesis 1:29 comes from the Priestly cosmogony with its sweeping, unrestricted grant of plant food. Genesis 2:17 is from the Yahwistic garden narrative with its specific prohibition that sets up the fall. Harmonizers correctly note that 'every tree' in 1:29 is a general category, while the prohibition in 2:17 is a specific exception, so the two statements could coexist in a single narrative. Archer, Mathews, and Walton all run this line. That works as a reconciliation if you're reading the text as a single authored work. But the two passages are structurally different enough that most critical scholars see them as independent traditions. In Genesis 1, the grant is universal and unqualified, spoken to 'them' (male and female together) as part of the cosmic ordering. In Genesis 2, the prohibition is given to the man before the woman even exists, framed as a direct threat of death. The Documentary Hypothesis treats these as P and J respectively, and the apparent contradiction evaporates only if you assume the redactor intended a coherent narrative in which 1:29 is silently overridden by 2:17. That's not impossible, but the tension is real enough that it shouldn't be waved away.
contradictions.scholarship: Richard Elliott Friedman, The Bible with Sources Revealed (HarperOne, 2003), pp. 33-37. Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary (Fortress, 1984), pp. 220-222. Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15 (WBC 1; Word, 1987), pp. 33-34, 62-63. Kenneth A. Mathews, Genesis 1-11:26 (NAC 1A; B&H, 1996), pp. 211-213, for the harmonization. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 68-69.

contradictions.question: What kind of animals may we eat?
contradictions.summary: The canon gives four different answers to what humans are allowed to eat. Genesis 1:29 gives a strictly vegetarian menu in Eden. Genesis 9:3 tells Noah after the flood that every moving thing that lives is now food. Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 pull the permission back and restrict Israel to specific clean species, banning pigs, shellfish, hares, camels, and a long list of others. Mark 7:18-20 and Matthew 15:11 then have Jesus declaring that nothing entering a person from outside can defile them, which Mark 7:19 glosses as 'thus he declared all foods clean.' Four mandates, four different scopes.
contradictions.commentary: Skeptics read this as four incompatible dietary rules in one book. Dispensationalists like Charles Ryrie and Robert Saucy read it as a single progressive revelation unfolding across four successive covenants: Edenic vegetarianism, Noahic concession to meat-eating, Mosaic restriction for Israel as a separated people, and Christian freedom under the New Covenant. Source critics read it as three or four distinct authorial voices that were never trying to speak with one voice in the first place. All three framings deserve to be on the table, because each one gets something right. The dispensational reading is internally coherent for believers, and it gives the right answer to the question of why the rules look different in different books. What it concedes under the surface, though, is exactly what the skeptic is pointing at: the rules change. 'Be a vegan' and 'eat anything that moves' are not the same instruction, and packaging the change as a covenantal stage-transition doesn't remove the shift, it just names it. From a critical-historical angle, the rules change because the authors aren't the same people. The Priestly vegetarianism of Genesis 1:29 is P's idealized picture of the peaceful original order, with humans and animals both eating only plants. P then accounts for real-world meat consumption with Genesis 9:3's post-flood grant to Noah, which is P again softening its own ideal. The Levitical kashrut of Leviticus 11 is Priestly and Holiness Code material doing systematic purity work, and Jacob Milgrom's three-volume Anchor Bible commentary on Leviticus walks through how the dietary restrictions function inside P's broader holiness logic. Deuteronomy 14 is a parallel but not identical list from the Deuteronomic legal tradition. And the Markan declaration is, by the nearly universal consensus of critical New Testament scholarship, a Markan editorial gloss. Joel Marcus in the Anchor Bible Mark 1-8 is explicit that 'cleansing all foods' (katharizon panta ta bromata) is the evangelist speaking, not a red-letter quotation of the historical Jesus. Jonathan Klawans's work on moral versus ritual impurity sharpens the point: the historical Jesus in Mark 7 is arguing that moral defilement matters more than ritual handwashing, not that kosher law is abrogated. The Markan community, writing decades later for a mixed Gentile audience, then universalized the saying. Ehrman's observation lands here too. If Jesus had actually cancelled kosher law during his ministry, the Jerusalem council debates in Acts 15 and Peter's rooftop vision in Acts 10 are incomprehensible as narratives — Peter wouldn't need a three-fold heavenly vision to convince him that Gentile food was clean. The harmonization reading works theologically if you're already committed to progressive revelation. The source-critical reading is parsimonious and explains the data without needing a covenantal scaffolding read back into the texts. That is of course a subjective call on the evidence, but the evidence points to multiple authors working out food law over centuries, not a single unchanging divine menu dispensed in stages.

contradictions.question: Who was Timnah?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 36:12 identifies Timna as a woman, specifically the concubine of Eliphaz son of Esau, who bore Amalek to him. 1 Chronicles 1:36 lists 'Timna' as one of the sons of Eliphaz alongside Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, and Amalek. Same name, same father, different gender and different relationship. The sister-of-Lotan verses in Genesis 36:22 and 1 Chronicles 1:39 are not a separate contradiction; they are additional genealogical detail about the same woman.
contradictions.commentary: The sharp contradiction here is Genesis 36:12 against 1 Chronicles 1:36, and it is a straightforward gender-and-relationship problem. In Genesis 36:12 Timna is a woman who is the concubine of Eliphaz and who bears him a son named Amalek. In 1 Chronicles 1:36 the Chronicler's list of Eliphaz's sons reads 'Teman, Omar, Zephi and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna and Amalek' — Timna appearing as one of Eliphaz's sons. A woman does not belong on the sons list, and a concubine is not a son. That is the actual tension. The Lotan's-sister verses (Gen 36:22 and 1 Chr 1:39) get sometimes swept into the contradiction as a third claim about Timna's identity, but they don't contradict Genesis 36:12 at all. A woman can be both Lotan's sister in her Horite family of origin and later the concubine of Eliphaz in her marital household. Those are just two biographical data points about the same person viewed from two genealogical angles. Folding them into the contradiction weakens the case, because it conflates a real textual problem with a non-problem. Keep the spotlight on Genesis 36:12 versus 1 Chronicles 1:36. Apologists handle the real contradiction a few ways. Archer and Keil-Delitzsch argue that 1 Chronicles 1:36 is elliptical: 'and Timna and Amalek' is short for 'and by Timna, Amalek,' drawing on Genesis 36:12's detail that Timna bore Amalek. This is a reasonable attempt, and it would harmonize the two lists if granted. The problem is that it requires inserting words that aren't in the Masoretic Text and treating a woman's name on a sons list as a prepositional phrase about her maternity. Sara Japhet in the Old Testament Library commentary notes that the Chronicler frequently condenses and occasionally garbles earlier genealogical material, and Gary Knoppers in the Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 1-9 points out that the Septuagint preserves variant readings in exactly this passage, reinforcing that the list shows signs of transmission trouble. The more parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler was working from a version of the Edomite genealogy that listed Timna differently, or that the text has been corrupted somewhere in its transmission. Either way, the contradiction between Genesis 36:12 and 1 Chronicles 1:36 as they now sit in the MT is real. The Lotan's-sister data isn't.

contradictions.question: Does God work on the Sabbath?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 2:2-3 has God resting on the seventh day after finishing creation and sanctifying that day as a day of rest. John 5:16-17 has Jesus explicitly declaring that 'my Father is working until now, and I also am working,' to defend Sabbath healing.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists typically solve this by distinguishing between two kinds of work: the creative labor of Genesis 1-2, which concluded with the cosmos complete, and the ongoing providential or redemptive activity referenced in John 5. Don Carson and Leon Morris both run this reading in their Johannine commentaries, pointing out that rabbinic tradition itself had already wrestled with the fact that God must continue to sustain the world on the Sabbath (birth, death, weather, etc.). On that reading, Genesis 2 is about the completion of creation, not a claim that God sits motionless every Saturday. This is a legitimate harmonization, and it's probably what John is doing theologically. The Johannine Jesus is appealing to a real rabbinic debate to justify his Sabbath healings. But the harmonization works at the theological level, not at the flat-textual level. Genesis 2:3 explicitly says God 'rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.' John 5:17 says God is working right now. As a historical-critical matter, the Johannine Jesus is effectively reinterpreting the Genesis rest in a way that the Priestly author probably wouldn't have recognized. The Fourth Gospel is using the claim polemically to blur the Father-Son distinction, which is exactly why 'the Jews' in John 5:18 want to kill him: he's making himself equal with God. The tension is real even if theologically reconcilable.

contradictions.question: Are the two creation accounts contradictory?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:25-27 places the creation of humans (male and female, simultaneously, in the image of God) after the animals as the climax of a structured six-day sequence. Genesis 2:18-22 has the man formed first and alone, animals then formed as a failed attempt to find him a helper, and the woman finally built from his rib. The same canonical text gives two incompatible orderings of creation and two incompatible methods of producing humanity.
contradictions.commentary: SAB's 'accounts.html' page isolates the Genesis 1 versus Genesis 2 doublet as the foundational creation contradiction, and it hits exactly the seam that the Documentary Hypothesis predicts. The Priestly author of Genesis 1 gives you a tightly structured cosmogony: light, sky, land, plants, luminaries, sea creatures and birds, land animals, humans as male-and-female together, Sabbath. The Yahwistic author of Genesis 2 gives you a completely different story shape: arid land with no rain, YHWH forming the adam from the adamah, garden planted for him, animals formed as potential helpers and paraded past him, woman finally constructed from a rib. Different order, different method, different divine name (Elohim versus YHWH Elohim), different literary register. Apologists like Archer, Mathews, Hamilton, and Walton argue that Genesis 2 is a 'zoom-in' on day six, a close-up view of the same events summarized in Genesis 1. Archer and the NIV translators lean on a pluperfect rendering of Genesis 2:19 ('had formed') to retroactively make the animals already exist. The problem is that the Hebrew wayyitzer is a standard waw-consecutive indicating narrative sequence, and the J narrative only makes sense if the animals are being freshly formed as candidate companions for a lonely man. You don't parade animals past Adam to find him a helper if they already exist elsewhere. James Kugel and Joel Baden have both pointed out that treating these as one story requires ignoring the actual literary signals. The simpler reading is the one Friedman and Baden describe: two independent creation traditions, P and J, stitched together by a later redactor who left the seams visible. The harmonization is theologically motivated; the two-source reading is parsimonious.

contradictions.question: How long did creation take?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:3-2:3 presents creation unfolding across six distinct days with a seventh day of rest. Genesis 2:4 refers to the whole thing happening in a single 'day' (beyom in Hebrew) when God made the earth and the heavens.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction evaporates on the apologetic reading that beyom in Genesis 2:4 is idiomatic Hebrew for 'when' rather than a specific 24-hour period. Archer, Sailhamer, and most evangelical Hebraists correctly note that the construction b-preposition plus infinitive construct does often function as a general temporal marker ('at the time when'). That's a reasonable linguistic point, and it probably does soften the apparent contradiction to some degree. But it doesn't fully eliminate it. Genesis 2:4a is generally recognized by critical scholars (Wellhausen, Friedman, Baden) as the colophon closing the Priestly creation account, while Genesis 2:4b is the incipit of the Yahwistic account. The two halves of Genesis 2:4 are from different sources, and the Yahwistic 'day' in 2:4b doesn't presuppose the six-day framework of the Priestly account at all. The J author simply has one event-day of creation with no structured week behind it. So the contradiction is less 'one day versus six days in a single narrative' and more 'two sources with different temporal frames got stitched together.' The apologetic idiomatic reading papers over the seam. It doesn't remove it. That's a subjective call on what counts as a contradiction, but the text-historical picture is clear.

contradictions.question: Were plants created before or after humans?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:11-13 creates vegetation on day three, before humans arrive on day six. Genesis 2:4-9 has God forming the man first, then planting the garden and causing every tree to grow, placing plants after the human.
contradictions.commentary: Same doublet problem. In P, plants arrive on day three, long before humans. In J, YHWH forms the man from the dust, then plants a garden, then makes trees grow for him. Genesis 2:5 is explicit: 'no plant of the field had yet sprung up, for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was no man to till the ground.' The J author isn't being ambiguous here. He's saying plants hadn't grown yet because there was no human to farm them. Apologists including Archer and Walton argue that Genesis 2:5 refers specifically to cultivated plants that require human farming, not wild vegetation, so the day-three creation of general plant life in Genesis 1 is compatible with the absence of cultivated crops in Genesis 2. That's an actually decent reading of the Hebrew siach ha-sadeh ('plant of the field') and eseb ha-sadeh ('herb of the field'), and it's what Cassuto, Kidner, and Walton all argue. But the harmonization works better for Genesis 2:5 than for 2:8-9, where YHWH 'planted a garden' and 'made every tree to grow' after forming the man. If the plant world of Genesis 1 was already in place, why does YHWH need to plant a new garden and grow new trees? The J text reads like a fresh act of vegetation creation, not a specialized horticultural addendum. The tension is genuine.

contradictions.question: Did God originally create humans male and female?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:27 and Jesus' citation of it in Matthew 19:4 state that God made humans 'male and female' from the beginning, as a simultaneous creation. Genesis 2:7, 2:18-20, and 2:21-22 instead describe the man being formed first, followed by a failed attempt to find him a helper among the animals, and only afterward the woman being built from his rib.
contradictions.commentary: Matthew 19:4 quotes Genesis 1:27 as if it were the authoritative description of human creation, but Genesis 2 tells an entirely different story in which Eve is a delayed afterthought. Apologists typically argue that Genesis 2 is a more detailed zoom-in on day six from the summary view of Genesis 1. Archer, Hamilton, and Mathews all take this line. The framing is that Genesis 1 gives the aerial photograph and Genesis 2 gives the close-up. The problem is that the two texts don't just differ in detail, they differ in order, method, and relational framing. Genesis 1 has a simultaneous dual creation of male and female as the climactic act. Genesis 2 has a sequential single creation of the man, followed by a narrative beat in which the man is alone, then animals are formed as a failed helper-search, then finally the woman is constructed from his rib. The two methods are incompatible: simultaneous creation in the divine image versus sequential derivation from the man's body. The Jesus of Matthew 19 reads Genesis 1:27 as the foundational statement for marriage, which works theologically but silently passes over the Genesis 2 contradiction. James Kugel and Phyllis Trible both treat this as a case where the final editor left the two traditions in tension rather than resolving them. The theological use of Genesis 1:27 has real consequences: if you take Genesis 2 as the original account, the hierarchical ordering is built into the text. If you take Genesis 1:27, it isn't.

contradictions.question: Is marriage a good thing?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 2:18-24 presents marriage as a divine solution to the problem that 'it is not good that man should be alone.' 1 Corinthians 7:1 and 7:7 have Paul declaring that 'it is good for a man not to touch a woman' and wishing that all men were unmarried like himself.
contradictions.commentary: This is a classic tension between the Genesis mandate for pair-bonding and Paul's apocalyptic-celibate outlook. Apologists rightly point out that Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 7 is shaped by his expectation of the imminent parousia and the 'present distress' (v. 26), so his preference for celibacy is situational, not a general denunciation of marriage. Craig Blomberg and Gordon Fee both emphasize this context, and Paul himself says marriage is not sin (v. 28) and encourages marriage for those who lack self-control (v. 9). So Paul is not saying marriage is bad; he's saying singleness is better under eschatological pressure. That's a real qualification, and the contradiction softens when you read Paul contextually. But it doesn't fully dissolve. The Genesis text frames marriage as an intrinsic good that addresses humanity's inherent need for companionship, with no eschatological qualifier. Paul's framing is that marriage is a concession to weakness, not the ideal. Dale Martin notes that Paul's valorization of celibacy introduced a new theological framework into the Jewish marriage-positive tradition, and that tension worked its way into later Christian asceticism. So the contradiction is softer than the bare question implies, but the evaluative framing of marriage absolutely shifts between Genesis and Paul.

contradictions.question: When was Eve created?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 1:27 has God creating male and female simultaneously on day six, in the divine image. Genesis 2:20-22 has Eve created separately, after Adam has already named all the animals, by YHWH taking one of Adam's ribs and fashioning her from it.
contradictions.commentary: Same doublet as the 'male and female' contradiction, and it's really a subset of the larger Genesis 1 / Genesis 2 problem. The Priestly account in chapter 1 has humans created together as a single act. The Yahwistic account in chapter 2 has the woman formed after the man, after the garden, and after the animals, as the solution to the man's loneliness when no suitable helper is found among the beasts. Apologists read this as two windows on a single event, with Genesis 2 filling in the details of Genesis 1's summary. Archer, Currid, and Mathews all run this line. The problem, again, is that the two texts describe two fundamentally different creation events. Genesis 1's simultaneous divine-image creation and Genesis 2's rib-derivation aren't different angles on the same moment; they're different stories. James Kugel's observation is that Second Temple Jewish interpreters noticed this contradiction and tried to solve it through the Adam-and-Lilith legend, where Adam had a first wife created with him in Genesis 1 (Lilith), who left him, and Eve was then made from the rib. That legend is rabbinic invention, but it exists precisely because the two texts don't fit together in a straightforward reading. The redactor of the Pentateuch left both accounts standing, and the tension has been generating interpretive work for 2,500 years. That's a subjective call on how to read redaction, but the textual data supports the critical reading.
contradictions.scholarship: James L. Kugel, Traditions of the Bible (Harvard, 1998), pp. 72-82, on Second Temple interpretations of the double creation. Richard Elliott Friedman, The Bible with Sources Revealed (HarperOne, 2003), pp. 33-37. Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary (Fortress, 1984), pp. 158-172, 225-234. Phyllis Trible, God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (Fortress, 1978), pp. 72-105. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 68-69. Alter, Robert, The Five Books of Moses (Norton, 2004), pp. 17-22, on the literary independence of the two accounts.

contradictions.question: Is wisdom a good thing?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and James repeatedly extol wisdom as supremely valuable, something to be pursued and preferred over gold. Genesis 3:6, Job 37:24, and 1 Corinthians 1:19 present wisdom as dangerous, rejected by God, or targeted for destruction.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction softens when you recognize that 'wisdom' in the Hebrew Bible and New Testament is not a single concept. The Proverbs tradition uses chokmah (Hebrew) or sophia (Greek) to mean reverent, God-fearing practical wisdom rooted in the fear of YHWH. That's the wisdom that gets praised. The 'wisdom' condemned in 1 Corinthians 1:19 (quoting Isaiah 29:14) is explicitly 'the wisdom of this world,' meaning Greco-Roman philosophical rhetoric that Paul sees as opposed to the cross. Apologists including Fee, Ciampa-Rosner, and Thiselton are right to note this distinction, and it does address the Paul citation. Similarly, Genesis 3:6 isn't a condemnation of wisdom in the abstract, it's a narrative about disobediently grasping wisdom outside God's permission. The real tension in this contradiction cluster isn't the big-picture theological evaluation of wisdom; it's more specific. Job 37:24 ('he respecteth not any that are wise of heart') is harder to harmonize, and Qoheleth's own wisdom skepticism (Ecclesiastes 1:18: 'in much wisdom is much grief, and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow') sits uneasily with Proverbs' unqualified endorsement. Michael Fox and James Crenshaw both treat Qoheleth as an intentional critic of Proverbs' confident wisdom theology. So the picture isn't 'wisdom is uniformly good' versus 'wisdom is uniformly bad.' It's that the canon preserves multiple wisdom traditions that evaluate wisdom differently, and the New Testament adds yet another layer by distinguishing divine wisdom from human wisdom. That's genuine internal diversity, not a flat contradiction.
contradictions.scholarship: Michael V. Fox, Ecclesiastes (JPS Bible Commentary, 2004), pp. xi-xxv. James L. Crenshaw, Old Testament Wisdom: An Introduction, 3rd ed. (WJK, 2010), pp. 139-166. Roland E. Murphy, The Tree of Life: An Exploration of Biblical Wisdom Literature, 3rd ed. (Eerdmans, 2002), pp. 49-71. Gordon D. Fee, The First Epistle to the Corinthians, rev. ed. (NICNT; Eerdmans, 2014), pp. 75-110. Anthony C. Thiselton, The First Epistle to the Corinthians (NIGTC; Eerdmans, 2000), pp. 150-180. Richard J. Clifford, Proverbs (OTL; WJK, 1999), pp. 19-28.
